diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone in the distal radius epimetaphysis
legend: An anteroposterior radiograph demonstrates an expansile osteolytic tumour with a well-defined, partly sclerotic margin. Note the extension up to the subchondral bone plate.

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone in the distal radius epimetaphysis
legend: MRI was performed 2 months after the radiograph in Fig. <<#53955>>, with an interval increase in tumour size. Coronal T1-weighted MRI shows a homogeneous intermediate signal intensity in the tumour.

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone in S1 and S2 of the sacrum
legend: Sagittal reformat of an unenhanced CT image at baseline demonstrates an osteolytic, expansile tumour with cortical destruction in the S1 and S2 vertebral bodies. There is no internal matrix mineralization.

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone in S1 and S2 of the sacrum
legend: After 4 months of neoadjuvant denosumab therapy, the tumour has become sclerotic internally, and neocortex formation is present.

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone; imaging and gross correlation of conventional giant cell tumour of bone
legend: The anteroposterior radiograph of this distal femur tumour (correlating with the gross specimen in Fig. <<53961>>) demonstrates an expansile osteolytic tumour with a sclerotic margin, abutting the subchondral plate.

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone; imaging and gross correlation of conventional giant cell tumour of bone
legend: The tumour grossly shows a red/tan, somewhat lobulated cut surface with a well-defined border.

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone after denosumab treatment
legend: Imaging and gross correlation. The anteroposterior radiograph of this distal radius giant cell tumour shows an expansile lesion with extensive mineralization, the latter of which is a typical consequence of denosumab treatment.

diagnosis: Conventional giant cell tumour of bone; histological features
legend: The tumour in an intramedullary lesion with a sharply demarcated border and regions of intratumoural haemorrhage.

diagnosis: Conventional giant cell tumour of bone; histological features
legend: In regions where the cortex is effaced, the tumour is instead surrounded by a rim of reactive woven bone and periosteum.

diagnosis: Conventional giant cell tumour of bone; histological features
legend: The tumour is composed of mononuclear neoplastic cells with numerous admixed non-neoplastic osteoclast-like giant cells, some of which have many nuclei.

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone
legend: Histological features of conventional giant cell tumour of bone. The neoplastic mononuclear cells show amphophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and distinct nucleoli. The nuclear features of the neoplastic cells appear similar to those of the osteoclast-like giant cells.

diagnosis: Conventional giant cell tumour of bone with benign fibrous histiocytoma–like morphology
legend: Some conventional giant cell tumours of bone show prominent spindle cell morphology, with short fascicles of bland spindle cells and numerous admixed foamy histiocytes. Such examples tend to lack osteoclast-like giant cells.

diagnosis: Conventional giant cell tumour of bone with benign fibrous histiocytoma–like morphology
legend: These tumours harbour just the same H3.3 G35W mutations that are detectable with mutation-specific antibodies, as shown here.

diagnosis: Conventional giant cell tumour of bone; histological features
legend: Necrosis can be seen in otherwise conventional giant cell tumours of bone as a less common feature, and in isolation it has no prognostic significance. Necrosis tends to occur in the setting of pathological fracture.

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone
legend: Less common histological features of conventional giant cell tumour of bone. Uncommonly, the leading edge of the tumour can show focal permeation of native trabeculae.

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone
legend: Less common histological features of conventional giant cell tumour of bone. Some examples of giant cell tumour of bone exhibit isolated nuclear atypia, which usually takes the form of scattered enlarged nuclei with somewhat smudgy chromatin and occasional nuclear pseudoinclusions. This atypia has no known prognostic significance in isolation.

diagnosis: Malignant giant cell tumour of bone
legend: Some malignant giant cell tumours of bone show an admixture of conventional components (left) and malignant components (right).

diagnosis: Malignant giant cell tumour of bone
legend: Most malignant giant cell tumours of bone show osteosarcomatous differentiation.

diagnosis: Malignant giant cell tumour of bone
legend: About 30% of malignant giant cell tumours of bone show chondrosarcomatous differentiation. This finding presents the pitfall for misdiagnosis of dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma.

diagnosis: Malignant giant cell tumour of bone
legend: Some malignant giant cell tumours of bone show regions resembling (malignant) chondroblastoma, with myxohyaline stroma and neoplastic cells with eccentric, folded nuclei.

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone in the distal radius epimetaphysis
legend: Axial T2-weighted Dixon MRI demonstrates typical heterogeneous signal intensity, with areas of very low signal due to haemosiderin, and small cystic areas (arrow). The tumour is seen expanding in between the extensor tendons (asterisks).

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone after denosumab treatment.
legend: Imaging and gross correlation. The tumour grossly shows a fibrous, sclerotic cut surface, consistent with extensive intralesional bone formation.

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone after denosumab treatment
legend: After long-term denosumab therapy, the treated tumours can show extensive bone formation, as seen in this example where neoplastic bone (right) merges with native trabecular bone (left) at the tumour periphery.

diagnosis: Giant cell tumour of bone
legend: Posteroanterior radiograph (shown here), axial T1-weighted imaging (Fig. <<56750>>), and coronal fat-saturated T2-weighted imaging (Fig. <<56751>>) of a giant cell tumour of the wrist. The radiograph demonstrates an expansile lesion that extends to the subarticular bone surface in a skeletally mature patient. This is of homogeneous low T1 signal and high T2 signal, with preserved surrounding cortex.
source: Dr Huw Walters and Dr Rajat Chowdhury, Department of Radiology, Nuffield Orthopaedic Centre, Oxford, UK

legend: This giant cell tumour of bone shows regions of "benign fibrous histiocytoma"-like morphology.

diagnosis: Bone Tumor
